What I need from you by EOD Thursday:
- Three reserve scenarios (conservative / balanced / aggressive) expressed as GPU-months and equivalent committed vCPU/GPU pools, with top-line monthly cost and expected per-token cost improvement.
- Any SLA / latency delta per scenario (e.g., 99th pct latency target, burst credits availability).
- Practical ramp constraints (how long to bring pools online, lead time, and capex/ops implications).

Thanks — short on time here, but this will make a big difference in the call.

Requested spreadsheet attached (reserve_scenarios_Q1Q2_2029.xlsx) — I filled a first pass with infra's conservative / balanced / aggressive GPU-month numbers for us-west-2 plus a note column for lead times. High-level callouts:

- Conservative: 40 GPU-months / modest burst pool. Lead time: 2–3 weeks to provision. Expected per-token cost savings: ~8–10% vs on-demand hosted. Will meet 95th/99th latency targets for small-medium prompts.
- Balanced: 120 GPU-months / burstable dedicated fleet plus prefix cache sizing. Lead time: ~4–6 weeks to stabilize. Cost savings: ~18–22% token-level. Targets: 99th pct latency ~ 220–240ms for standard LLMs; supports initial canary for new models.
- Aggressive: 300 GPU-months / larger reserved pools across two AZs + burst credits. Lead time: 8–12 weeks for full redundancy. Cost savings: ~30%+ at scale; supports strict 99th pct latency < 200ms for most workloads.

Assumptions: 1) these are NVL-1 style GPU equates (mixed 80% A100-equivalent profile); 2) forecasting uses ACME's current projected Q1 token run rate with 35% expected growth month-over-month; 3) burst credits are finite and recommended only for short-term spikes.

Open Qs for Laura: what discount bands trigger additional committed-credit offsets and what billing cadence (monthly vs quarterly) will procurement prefer? I also noted two low-confidence deals in the pipeline that materially swing the balanced->aggressive numbers — marked in the sheet.

Ben
Ben Carter
Head of Fleet Planning, Redwood Inference

Thanks Ben — spreadsheet looks great. I pulled pricing/discount constraints into the second tab and sketched a simple P&L delta for each scenario. Highlights:

- Conservative: low cash impact; we can price as a modest uplift on hosted list. Minimal discount; procurement may sign quickly.
- Balanced: requires a committed spend threshold (~$120k/month) to unlock a 15% blended discount across token costs and reduce peak billing variance. This is our recommended starting point for ACME if they want meaningful unit economics while keeping optionality.
- Aggressive: meaningful revenue commitment; needs legal to approve a multi-quarter SLA with redundancy language. Finance will need a 30–60 day out clause tied to usage if we bake in deeper discounts.

Other notes: billing cadence preference will often be monthly with a quarterly reconciliation clause. If ACME requests invoice-netting or 3rd-party financing, that will push procurement timelines ~2 weeks. I also flagged GAAP revenue recognition notes on the Aggressive scenario (we'll need a revenue ops touch).

Attached: MAP-draft-Acme.pdf (mutual action plan draft) with suggested milestones: PO signature -> staging validation -> production cutover -> review/QoS checkpoint.

Laura

All — great alignment, thanks. Quick summary and asks before our Friday conversation at 10am PT (invite sent):

Summary of recommended ask to ACME (we'll present three options):
1) Conservative: 40 GPU-months, monthly billing, quick start (2–3 weeks). Minimal discount (~5–8%). Good for customers who want SLA-lite guarantees.
2) Balanced (recommended): 120 GPU-months, monthly billing with quarterly reconciliation, 15% blended discount, SLA with 99th pct target ~230ms, canary window and 4–6 week ramp.
3) Aggressive: 300 GPU-months, multi-AZ redundancy, 30%+ discount with stricter SLA; finance requires a 30–60 day out clause for recognition. Longer lead time (8–12 weeks).
